legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Towards Compute-Optimal Many-Shot In-Context Learning", Golchin, Chen, Han, Gandhi, Yu, Mishra, Surdeanu, Agarwal, Lee, Pfister (Univ. of Arizona, Google Cloud AI Research, Google DeepMind). COLM 2025 (arXiv 2507.16217v2, 29 Aug 2025).

COVERAGE: Pages 1-24 of 24 read (about 1,075 extracted lines). Main text is pp. 1-9. Pp. 10-13 are references (skimmed). Pp. 14-24 are appendix prompt examples (Figs 6-19), with no result tables. Numbers were read from the text only. The results are in Figs 2, 4 and 5, which are images, so I did not read their per-point values.

CENTRAL CLAIM: Many-shot ICL usually uses a fixed random demonstration set so it can be cached. Similarity selection beats random but breaks caching and costs quadratic compute. The paper's fix is a hybrid. It uses a small number (s=20) of per-query similar demos plus a large cached block of random demos (or k-means-chosen demos). This matches or beats pure similarity selection at far lower cost.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Hybrid similarity-random and similarity-k-means match or beat the best baseline (similarity-only) at much lower proportional inference cost.
  number: "nearly two times lower in 50-shot settings and ten times lower in 200-shot settings"
  setup: Gemini 1.5 Pro (gemini-1.5-pro-002) and Gemini 2.0 Flash (gemini-2.0-flash-001), temperature 0. Datasets are ANLI r3, TREC (50 labels), GSM Plus and MetaTool, with 1,000 test samples each. n in {0,50,100,150,200}, always s=20 similar demos. The cached part (r or k) is 30/80/130/180. Cost is proportional, derived from attention complexity. It is not dollars or measured latency.
  quote: "Both of our selection strategies match the similarity-based approach in cases where it delivers the highest performance. In some datasets, such as ANLI and MetaTool, our strategies even outperform it. However, this level of performance in our methods is achieved with substantially lower inference costs—nearly two times lower in 50-shot settings and ten times lower in 200-shot settings."
  where: p.7, Sec 4.3
- On TREC at 50 shots, similarity-k-means beats the k-means-with-mapping baseline while cost is halved (relative to similarity-only).
  number: ">11% Flash, >6% Pro", cost halved
  setup: 50-shot, TREC, Gemini Flash and Pro. The paper does not say whether the gain is absolute or relative. It says the hybrid rises to the level of similarity-only.
  quote: "In the 50-shot setting, this improvement is more than 11% with Gemini Flash and over 6% with Gemini Pro, while the inference cost is cut in half."
  where: p.8, Sec 4.3
- The benefit of a selection criterion fades as shots grow, so random demos approach similarity-selected ones.
  number: none (the TREC plateau is at 50 shots)
  setup: Fig 4, both models. The paper says the effect shows on ANLI, GSM Plus and MetaTool. TREC needs more than 200 shots to converge.
  quote: "on the TREC dataset, the performance of the similarity-based selection strategy for both models remains almost unchanged beyond the 50-shot setting, whereas performance under random selection continues to improve, especially between 150 and 200 shots."
  where: p.7, Sec 4.2
- Cost model: similarity-only prompts cannot be cached, so cost is O(n^2). Cached random or k-means prompts cost O(ct+t^2), which is about O(ct) since c≫t. Hybrids cost O(c(s+t)+(s+t)^2), which is about O(c(s+t)).
  number: none
  setup: c = avg cached tokens, t = avg test tokens, s = avg similar-demo tokens. Model size is a constant multiplier. KV caching (Pope et al. 2023) is assumed, though the method is stated to be independent of the caching implementation.
  quote: "Therefore, our proposed hybrid selection strategies scale linearly with the average number of cached tokens, i.e., O(c), similar to random or k-means-based selection methods with fully cached content."
  where: p.6, Sec 4.1
- Low-data regime: with a pool of only 100 demos, using 20-80 similar demos plus random or k-means for the rest beats using the whole pool.
  number: "about 3%–6%"
  setup: BBH Geometric Shapes, Logical Deduction (7 objects) and Salient Translation Error Detection. Pool = 100 random samples and test = 150 per task. Fixed at 100 shots, similar demos varied 20 to 80. Similar demos are sampled with replacement relative to the random ones, so repeats occur.
  quote: "adjusting the proportion of similar demonstrations can lead to performance gains of about 3%–6% over using the full pool."
  where: p.9, Sec 4.4
- The proportion of demos picked by each criterion works as a cost/performance hyperparameter.
  number: none
  quote: "the proportion of demonstrations selected based on each criterion can serve as a hyperparameter to balance performance and inference cost in many-shot ICL settings."
  where: p.8
- Test-informed k-means helps. Centroids come from test-sample embeddings, then map to the nearest demos. Beyond the k-means-without-mapping baseline, this adds performance at about the same cost.
  number: none
  quote: "When centroid mapping from test data is applied in the k-means strategy, performance improves further with almost no additional inference cost."
  where: p.7
- Neither hybrid is universally best, but costs are nearly identical.
  number: none
  quote: "there is no single universally best performer across all datasets and settings."
  where: p.7
- On MetaTool, similarity-only gave no gain over zero-shot, while random helped and the hybrid exceeded random.
  number: none
  quote: "the similarity-based strategy does not enhance performance compared to the zero-shot setting"
  where: p.7
- Demo order is treated as negligible in many-shot, citing Bertsch et al. 2024, so demos were randomly ordered with no ordering study.
  where: p.5

SETUP DETAILS: Gecko embeddings (text-embedding-004, 768-d, cosine, SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY). Default scikit-learn k-means, with k in 1-20 chosen by the elbow method. Max completion is 20 tokens for non-generative tasks and 8,000 for generative ones. Up to 100,000 train samples form the demo pool. Baselines: random, similarity, k-means with mapping, k-means without mapping.

LIMITS
- Cost is proportional and theoretical (attention complexity), not measured dollars or latency. The paper says "Due to the proprietary nature of our LLMs ... we analyze proportional inference costs instead of absolute values". It does not model provider cache-pricing discounts, cache TTL or prefill versus decode.
- Only Gemini 1.5 Pro and 2.0 Flash, with a shared tokenizer. Only 4 tasks plus 3 BBH tasks. Max 200 shots, which is "many-shot" only modestly (Agarwal used up to thousands).
- k-means needs the test set in advance. A footnote says it can be applied progressively as test samples arrive. The cluster count is tuned on test data, which is a leakage-style caveat.
- Some of the performance gap is small or inconsistent. TREC needs more than 200 shots for random to catch up. The authors do not report variance, seeds or significance tests in the text.
- The headline "order of magnitude" cost cut is at 200 shots on the cost model. The 2x figure at 50 shots is the lower end.
- No explicit limitations section. The paper uses reasoning in Sec 4.4 to argue that repetition helps, whereas Agarwal et al. found repetition does not help.

BUILDS ON
- Agarwal et al. 2024 (Many-shot ICL, arXiv 2404.11018) and Bertsch et al. 2024 (In-context learning with long-context models, arXiv 2405.00200). Both are credited for the observation that selection criteria matter less at scale and random selection is preferred.
- Also: Brown et al. 2020 (ICL), Liu et al. 2021 (similarity-based selection, "What makes good in-context examples"), An et al. 2023 (diversity), Baek et al. 2024, Pope et al. 2023 (KV caching), Thorndike 1953 (elbow method), Lee et al. 2024 (Gecko), Zhao et al. 2021, Lu et al. 2021 and Zhang et al. 2022 (ordering), Jiang et al. 2024 (multimodal many-shot).

CODE: none in the paper. Prompt layout, Fig 1 and Appendix A: cached block = instruction + [random or k-means demos]. Dynamic suffix = [20 similar demos] + test sample. Cached/dynamic pairs are in Figs 6/7 (ANLI), 8/9 (TREC), 10/11 (GSM Plus), 12/13 (MetaTool), 14-19 (BBH).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): the many-shot prompt format. Hatched blocks are cached and solid blocks are not. Shows that only the small similar-demo block is recomputed. It is the fastest way to see the mechanism and the proportions.
- Fig 2 (p.2): Pareto plots of performance versus proportional inference cost across datasets for Gemini Pro and Flash, comparing the hybrids against the baselines. It is the best single picture of the central claim: the hybrids sit on the frontier.
- Fig 4 (p.6) has the per-shot-count performance curves and the cost curves (3 rows). Fig 5 (p.8) has the BBH low-data bars. Fig 3 (p.4) illustrates the k-means mapping.

PROBLEMS: None with extraction. Figure values are images and were not extracted, so no per-dataset accuracy numbers are reported. No embedded instructions found in the text.

TARGET NOTE FIT: ai-engineering/01-prompt-engineering/notes/03-core-techniques.md, in the few-shot / many-shot ICL and example-selection section, specifically the cost and caching trade-off of dynamic (similarity) versus fixed (random) examples. It sharpens the existing claims from Agarwal 2024 and Bertsch 2024 that at high shot counts selection matters less, with a cacheable-prefix-plus-dynamic-suffix recipe.
